The problem it solves is checking membership, or finding what an element pairs with, without a nested loop. Two Sum asks for two elements that add to a target; checking every pair against every other is O(n²), and it repeats work a single pass could remember instead, since once you have seen a value, answering whether you have also seen its complement should cost no more than one more lookup.

The mechanism is recording each element in the table as you go, and checking the table before you add to it: for element i, compute the value that would complete the pair, look it up among the elements already seen, and only afterwards record the current element itself, so nothing pairs with itself and a repeated value is still found. Each lookup is O(1) on average, because ordinary keys spread across the buckets so each one holds about one element, and the table keeps that average, its
, at or below 1 by rehashing into more buckets as it grows, which keeps insertion amortised O(1) too.

What it costs is the word average: when many keys collide into one bucket, from a poor hash or from keys chosen to attack it, a lookup degrades to O(n) and the whole pass becomes O(n²), a bound the table does not guard against the way a balanced tree's O(log n) does.
